chief_complaint: sunken chest appearance causing exertional dyspnea in teen
hpi_details: A 17-year-old male presents with a sunken chest appearance and exertional dyspnea. The deformity has become more noticeable during adolescence.
ideas: He thinks his breastbone and ribs grew inward abnormally during his recent growth spurt and are mechanically pressing on his lungs when he runs.
concerns: He is worried that his breathing trouble will force him to quit the varsity soccer team and miss out on athletic college recruitment.
expectations: He hopes to find out whether targeted exercises or a chest brace can correct the dip without needing metal bars put in his chest.
social_hx: No tobacco, alcohol, or drug use; high school student, plays on the soccer team.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pectus Excavatum is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Assessment includes chest-wall imaging to characterize severity and selective cardiopulmonary testing for symptomatic patients; surgical repair is considered for significant physiologic impairment or substantial symptoms after specialist evaluation.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Pectus Excavatum.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Anxiety-related exercise intolerance without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Palpitations or chest pain with exertion.
management_principles: Characterize deformity severity with appropriate imaging and selectively assess cardiopulmonary impact; refer to chest-wall surgery to discuss repair when physiologic impairment or substantial symptoms are present
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A congenital chest wall deformity with a sunken sternum, causing exertional breathlessness in a teenager when severe enough to compress the heart or lungs.
red_flags: Palpitations or chest pain with exertion

must_ask.say: When did you first notice the sunken chest, and has it gotten worse?
How does this affect your breathing during sports?
How does this make you feel about your appearance?
What are you hoping the surgery will change?

history.answer: My chest looks sunken inward, and lately I've been getting short of breath whenever I run or play soccer.
I've had a slight dip in my chest since I was younger, but it became much deeper and more noticeable over the past two years during my growth spurt.
It is right in the center of my lower breastbone area, like an indented hollow in the middle of my chest.
I feel winded and like I cannot take a deep, full breath when I push myself physically.
I play on the high school soccer team, and over the past several months I tire out much faster and cannot keep up with my teammates during full drills.
The dent definitely got noticeably deeper as I grew taller over the last couple of years.
Running hard, sprints, and intense soccer practice bring on the shortness of breath.
Stopping the activity and resting for five to ten minutes helps my breathing return completely to normal.
No, I do not get chest pain or pressure, just the feeling of running out of air.
No, I haven't felt fluttering, racing, or pounding in my chest.
No, I have never passed out, blacked out, or felt lightheaded while running.
No, I don't have any cough, and I have never heard myself wheezing.
No, I have not had any fever or chills.
No, my weight has been steady and I don't have night sweats.
I have not seen a doctor for this before or had any chest x-rays done yet.
I tried doing some posture exercises and push-ups, but they didn't change the hollow in my chest or help my breathing during runs.
No, I don't have allergies to dust or pollen, and breathing cold air doesn't trigger this.
It is affecting my soccer play because I have to sit out for breaks sooner, which is really frustrating.
history.topic: Impact on sports and daily activities

history.answer: It makes me feel self-conscious when taking my shirt off in the locker room, and I worry about how it looks.
I shot up four inches last year, so I think my breastbone just grew inward abnormally and is pressing against my lungs when I sprint.
I'm worried that my endurance will keep dropping and I'll get kicked off the varsity soccer team before college scouts come to watch.
I'm hoping you can give me some targeted exercises or a corrective brace so I don't have to get invasive surgery with metal bars.
I've always been healthy and have no chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or supplements.
I don't have any known drug allergies.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or vaped.
No, I do not drink alcohol or use any recreational drugs.
I'm a junior in high school and I live with my parents.
No one in my family has a sunken chest, heart problems, or lung conditions that I know of.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Athletic adolescent male sitting comfortably in no acute distress, with normal respiratory effort at rest.
Marked depression of the lower sternum and anterior chest wall without chest wall tenderness or crepitus.
Resonant percussion notes throughout all lung fields bilaterally.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs heard.
Normal spinal curvature without scoliosis, kyphosis, or midline spinal tenderness.
No peripheral edema, digital clubbing, or cyanosis in the extremities.
